tier_reason: Issue #1337 (opened 2019-09-29 by user cjdb) shows Google Benchmark tables where range_common beats the 'handrolled' row (marked '# base') at -O2 and -O3, but the handrolled and algorithm code, the compiler and the CPU model are not given, so this is a measurement without full methodology: C, not A or B.

corrections.baseline: the issue's 'handrolled' implementation, marked '# base' in the reporter's table (its code is not shown, so it is not known to be a plain loop); the 'algorithm' row is a further comparison whose code is not shown either
corrections.caveats: Weak evidence for a speed win. The numbers come from a bug report titled 'ranges::to is significantly slower than direct construction' (opened 2019-09-29), not from a project claim; the README makes no performance claim and publishes no numbers. The repo's perf/range_conversion.cpp reproduces only the range_common and range_to functions from the issue (Words/RangeCommon vs Words/RangeTo), with no hand-rolled baseline. The win over the hand-rolled row is one workload, 13% at -O2 and 3% at -O3 (likely noise level) on a 2-CPU machine; the compiler is not stated and the bodies of the handrolled and algorithm functions are not shown, so what they do is unknown. The library version tested predates current releases. The maintainer's run (8 CPUs at 2900 MHz, -O3) only compared Words/RangeCommon 201,502,562 ns with Words/RangeTo 241,609,633 ns. No comparison against std::ranges was found. Reachable third-party results go the other way: the transrangers README (Clang 11.0, GCC 11.1, Visual Studio 2019, run on a GitHub Action VM, flags and CPU not stated, times normalized to Range-v3) says transrangers is generally equivalent to handwritten code on Clang and consistently outperforms Range-v3 by a large factor there, that handwritten code and transrangers are generally faster than Range-v3 on Visual Studio except test 1, and that Range-v3 performs very badly on test 2 (concat|take|filter|transform) in all compilers; on GCC tests 4 and 6 fluctuate run to run. Issue #668 ('Poor performance compared to STL', 2017-2019) has a maintainer note that a partial_sum benchmark from a Stack Overflow question was still about half the speed of the STL approach (no compiler or flags). Lead from the books: no timings are given there. Tier C with low confidence.

notes: All numbers in claimed_speedup match the issue tables exactly; last commit 2026-10-10, BSL-1.0, 4.4k stars confirmed. Category 'sequence-containers' looks off for a ranges/views library (the measured object is a view pipeline copied into a vector); consider a ranges/algorithms category override. Transrangers caveat reworded to what the README literally says.

tier_reason: Independent third-party evaluation by tenstorrent engineers with public harness code (tests/tt_stl/move_only_function_bench/bench.cpp at ef313b0), compilers gcc-12 and clang-20 and the CMake Release build type stated, results checked in at commit ef313b0; no CPU model is given, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: BM_MoveOnlyCapture, median ns over 5 repetitions, std::function holding a shared_ptr wrapper vs zoo: gcc-12/libstdc++ 42.69 (3 allocs) vs 13.43; clang-20/libstdc++ 43.29 vs 14.00; clang-20/libc++ 45.64 vs 12.72 (about 3.2x, 3.1x and 3.6x faster, derived from page data); README: 'About 3x faster, 3 allocations down to 1.' BM_QueueThroughput (enqueue 1024 then drain), median ns per iteration, lower is better, std vs zoo: 5519.25 vs 5073.65, 6633.06 vs 5609.81, 7068.30 vs 5697.49 (about 1.09x, 1.18x and 1.24x faster, derived from page data). BM_ConstructInvokeDestroy small inline capture, std vs zoo: 2.66 vs 2.35, 2.64 vs 2.30, 2.63 vs 2.33 ns (about 1.13-1.15x, derived from page data; the README sums it up as 2.3-3.2 ns for all three candidates). Mixed elsewhere in results/summary.txt: BM_MoveConstruct small capture std 2.34 vs zoo 3.74 ns (gcc-12/libstdc++) and 2.34 vs 6.91 ns (clang-20/libstdc++), zoo slower; BM_MoveAssign large capture under libc++ std 14.76 vs zoo 17.62 ns, zoo slower; BM_MoveAssign boundary and large capture under clang-20/libstdc++ std 20.73 and 21.12 vs zoo 14.32 and 14.63 ns, zoo faster. Compile time, 300 instantiations, best of 3, std vs zoo: 3.67s vs 3.58s, 2.79s vs 2.53s, 7.46s vs 2.88s. Object .text bytes std vs zoo: 5229 vs 3111, 3256 vs 2114, 3633 vs 2108.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++-12 with libstdc++, clang++-20 with libstdc++, clang++-20 with -stdlib=libc++; C++20; README build commands pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (the CMakeLists also defaults to Release) and set no other optimization flags; google-benchmark v1.9.1, fu2 4.2.5, zoo pinned at commit 7fb5eed6331651e9d94c0f7e9017f2d56ba4b993; bench run with --benchmark_repetitions=5; harness bench.cpp as of commit ef313b0
corrections.workload: Third-party Google Benchmark harness in tenstorrent/tt-metal PR #57569 (issue #57444): std::function<void()> vs zoo::Function<zoo::AnyContainer<zoo::Policy<void*[kInlinePointers], zoo::Destroy, zoo::Move, zoo::RTTI>>, void()> vs fu2::function_base, all pinned to std::function's inline capacity; construct/invoke/destroy, move-construct and move-assign at small, boundary and large capture sizes, a move-only (unique_ptr) capture, queue throughput over 1024 jobs, plus compile time and object size.
corrections.caveats: Evidence is independent but not the project's own: the repo's benchmark/catch2Functions.cpp compares zoo::function against std::function, folly::Function and a function pointer but publishes no numbers, and the README contains none. The 3x figure is against std::function plus a shared_ptr workaround for a move-only capture, an idiom gap; the harness README notes std::move_only_function was unavailable in its toolchains, so the fair baseline was not measured. The measured type is zoo::Function over AnyContainer with the RTTI affordance (bench.cpp at ef313b0 says zoo::VTableFunction was deliberately not used); an earlier harness commit, b28acab, used zoo::VTableFunction<kInlinePointers, void()>, but the checked-in results include BoundaryCapture rows that exist only in the later harness. Results are mixed outside the headline rows: zoo is slower than std::function on small-capture move construction under libstdc++ (3.74 vs 2.34 ns on gcc-12, 6.91 vs 2.34 ns on clang-20) and on large-capture move assignment under libc++ (17.62 vs 14.76 ns). CPU model not stated; flags are only the CMake Release build type. The harness commits carry a Claude co-author line, and commit 103f9f0 later removed the checked-in result files, saying the data moves to a PR comment, so the commit-time numbers may be superseded by a rerun. zoo does not compile under -fno-rtti (per the harness README). PR #57569 is still open and unmerged: an intermediate commit (6b4a4e7) was 'backed by zoo', but the current head ships an in-house ttsl::move_only_function that adapts zoo's and LLVM unique_function's designs; the PR description's table (42.94 ns vs 12.96 ns on gcc-12) measures that in-house type, not zoo, so it is not used here. Queue-throughput gains are small (9-24%). The book lead matches the repo only by author name. Category changed from small-buffer-and-strings to smart-pointers-and-refcount because the compared facility is std::function (spec Part 3 map).

notes: Main fix: record said the benchmark measured zoo::VTableFunction<2, void()>; the results at ef313b0 come from bench.cpp using zoo::Function<AnyContainer<Policy<..., RTTI>>> (VTableFunction was only in earlier harness b28acab). Queue-throughput unit confirmed as median ns (lower is better), so the zoo win stands. License MIT, 139 stars, last commit 2026-04-15 (docs) confirmed; the Snapchat production claim in stars_or_usage was not checked and left as is.
